stories.title: Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 100 percent leased, Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California. Spear Street Capital was the buyer in the $121.5 million transaction. Tishman Speyer developed the 138,000-square-foot property in 2002 and immediately leased the office space in full to Fenwick & West, which has remained a customer in the building. Tishman Speyer claims the transaction represents one of the strongest pricing outcomes for a Mountain View office sale in recent years. Centrally located with convenient access to highways and Caltrain, 400 Castro features expansive roof decks, underground parking and views of the San Francisco Bay and coastal mountains. The property, which was 100% leased at the time of the sale, is located in the heart of Downtown Mountain View, surrounded by restaurants and retail, with Cascal restaurant, Peet’s Coffee, and Sweetgreen on site. Tishman Speyer was represented by the Eastdil Secured team led by Nate Jones. The post Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, Mountain View office, $121.5M to Spear Street Capital
100% leased Class A, 138K SF, single tenant (Fenwick & West) since 2002 delivery
Sale claimed 'one of strongest pricing outcomes' for Mountain View office in recent years
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer exited a fully leased, trophy office asset in Mountain View for $121.5M, marking what the developer called peak pricing for the submarket. The 138,000-SF Class A property, leased to law firm Fenwick & West since its 2002 delivery, changed hands to Spear Street Capital. The transaction signals office sellers are still finding liquidity and strong valuations in premium Silicon Valley trophy assets despite broader office headwinds.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. However, the 'strong pricing' narrative for stabilized office in Mountain View may be masking weak office fundamentals and cap-rate compression in trophy assets; it reflects capital still chasing quality but not necessarily broader market health. Watch for office-to-residential conversions in similar Mountain View/Silicon Valley Class A buildings as secondary leasing dynamics deteriorate.

stories.title: Sudberry Properties Inks $81.6M Refi on Growing Chula Vista Business Park
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged $81.6 million in financing for Otay River Business Park, a 369,803-square-foot industrial and retail business park located at 2925-2945 Main St. and 2775-2970 Faivre St. in Chula Vista, California. JLL worked on behalf of the borrower, Sudberry Properties, to secure a floating-rate, five-year loan through a debt fund. The loan includes future funding for construction completion and leasing costs. The property is positioned just east of Interstate 5 in Chula Vista. The development comprises stabilized, recently delivered and under-construction components across multiple phases built between 2021 and 2026. Phase IV, currently under construction, includes a 66,000-square-foot industrial building and parking facilities. The development is currently 100% leased across its existing space, with Phase IV already 70% pre-leased to an investment-grade tenant. The tenant base includes a diverse mix of industrial, distribution and retail users. The JLL Capital Markets team was led by Aldon Cole and Bharat Madan, along with Jenna Frakes. The post Sudberry Properties Inks $81.6M Refi on Growing Chula Vista Business Park appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sudberry Properties refinanced Otay River Business Park, Chula Vista, $81.6M floating-rate, 5-year
369K SF industrial/retail, 100% leased existing space, Phase IV 66K SF 70% pre-leased to investment-grade tenant
Multi-phase delivery 2021–2026 with construction completion and leasing funding included
stories.summary: Sudberry Properties secured $81.6M in floating-rate financing through JLL for Otay River Business Park in Chula Vista, a phased industrial-retail development east of I-5. The 370K-SF project is fully leased across completed phases and 70% pre-leased on Phase IV (66K SF under construction). The loan includes future funding for construction and leasing, signaling strong lender confidence in the submarket and tenant demand.
stories.impact: Strong industrial demand in Chula Vista (San Diego County) is pulling capital and financing—a leading indicator that logistics, distribution, and light industrial users are confident in the I-5 corridor and Southern California supply chains. Multifamily developers should note: concentrated industrial build-out and pre-leasing in tight supply windows suggests robust job and wage growth ahead in Chula Vista; acquisition/entitlement windows for renter-serving multifamily adjacent to industrial clusters (e.g., near I-5 nodes) may tighten as land scarcity increases.

stories.title: AI Growth Propels Tech to 2nd Place in NYC’s Office Leasing Frenzy
stories.excerpt: Technology has become New York City’s second most active leasing sector, behind finance, as the AI boom takes an expanding bite out of the Big Apple’s office supply, according to a new JLL report. Finance, law and tech now account for more than 70% of the city’s leasing activity year-to-date, up from an average of 50% throughout the 2010s. Tech firms leased a total of 1.1 million square in the third quarter, with AI companies driving more than 60% of that total, JLL found. The trend of traditional media and advertising firms evolving into tech businesses pushed the sector to overtake legal as the city’s number two engine of leasing activity. Overall, companies leased out 1.5 million square feet of space in August and 22.5 million square feet during the year to date. Asking rents continue to rise across all office classes as availability has dropped below 12.5% for the first time since 2018. Average direct asking rents have climbed to $86.71 per square foot, while total available space has contracted to 58.2 million square feet. “With much of the new construction already spoken for, speculative development is back in the conversation, while owners of existing buildings are moving quickly to reposition their properties,” noted Joe Sipala, managing director at JLL in a statement. “As demand for high-end quality space is surpassing supply, the race now is to see who can deliver the next generation of space.” The post AI Growth Propels Tech to 2nd Place in NYC’s Office Leasing Frenzy appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tech (AI-driven) now NYC's 2nd largest office leasing sector, 1.1M SF in Q3, 60% from AI firms
Finance, law, tech account for 70% YTD leasing activity vs. 50% average in 2010s
Office availability dropped below 12.5% for first time since 2018; asking rents at $86.71/SF
stories.summary: Technology firms—led by AI companies—leased 1.1M SF in Q3 and now rank second only to finance in NYC office activity. AI companies drove over 60% of tech leasing, pushing the sector to overtake legal. Finance, law, and tech now represent 70% of YTD leasing (up from 50% historical average), while overall availability has fallen below 12.5% and average rents climbed to $86.71/SF.
stories.impact: Explosive AI and tech hiring in Manhattan is creating acute office space competition and raising the cost of occupancy for tech talent—a strong demand signal for renter-serving multifamily in Manhattan submarkets with tech concentration (Flatiron, Midtown South, Hudson Square). Rising office rents and supply scarcity may accelerate office-to-residential conversions (especially Class B/C space), expanding the pool of newer, higher-quality residential supply. Multifamily developers should prioritize acquisition and entitlement in tech-dense neighborhoods; wage inflation in AI/tech roles supports premium rents and long-term lease stability.

stories.title: Related Secures $65M Refi for Office Property in L.A.’s South Bay
stories.excerpt: The owners of a 301,000-square-foot Class A office property in Los Angeles’ South Bay have secured refinancing for the property. Owners Related Companies and Cruzan landed the $64.7 million loan from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the eight-story property called the Torrance, named after its home city. The asset at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard is 93 percent occupied, according to Yardi Matrix, with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Salon Republic, Barrister Executive Suites, Compass California, Unio Health Partners and Morgan Stanley. Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Nick Scribani and Chris Lozinak arranged the debt. The property was built in 1988. Related and Cruzan acquired it from Stream Realty Partners for $106.8 million in 2017, and secured $59.2 million in refinancing in 2022. The South Bay has benefited from surging demand from aerospace and defense users for both office and industrial space. But the Greater Los Angeles office market remains deeply bifurcated. Overall vacancy was at 25.3 percent after the second quarter, nearly unchanged from year-end 2025, while trophy properties have a 13.5 percent vacancy rate, according to Newmark research. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Related and Cruzan secured $64.7M refi on 301K SF Class A office in Torrance (South Bay)

stories.summary: Related Companies and Cruzan refinanced the Torrance, a 301K-SF Class A office tower in Los Angeles' South Bay, for $64.7M through Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life. The property, acquired in 2017 for $106.8M and carrying a 93% occupancy rate, reflects strong tenant demand from aerospace and defense users driving office and industrial activity in the submarket.
stories.impact: Aerospace and defense sector expansion in LA South Bay (driven by Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing supply chains, and government spending) is fueling both office and industrial demand. Multifamily developers should view South Bay job growth—particularly wage premiums in aerospace/defense—as a secular demand tailwind for rental housing. The bifurcation of LA office (South Bay strong; broader LA weak) suggests renter-serving multifamily near aerospace/defense employment hubs will outperform; prioritize land in Torrance, El Segundo, Manhattan Beach, Hawthorne submarkets for multifamily upside.

stories.title: LG Group Plans Expansion in Major Markets, Announces Leadership Changes
stories.excerpt: Chicago-based LG Group announced a new company structure designed to support its next phase of growth, along with the appointment of Brett Carucci as the company’s chief operating officer. Under the new structure, LG Group will operate across two core business platforms, including integrated development and commercial general contracting. LG Group expects to begin more than $500 million in new development through its integrated development platform next year, along with another $100 million in general contracting. The company has already expanded its workforce by 10% and plans to grow by approximately 30% over the next year. Carucci brings more than two decades of experience in construction, development and project delivery. Most recently, he served as senior vice president of construction at Onni Group. He previously held leadership roles at Power Construction, DDR Corp. and The Beck Group. Outside Chicago, LG Group is focused on continued growth in Nashville and Phoenix, where it has completed projects, while pursuing additional development and construction opportunities in major markets nationwide. The post LG Group Plans Expansion in Major Markets, Announces Leadership Changes appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: LG Group (Chicago-based) plans $500M+ integrated development, $100M general contracting next year
Workforce expansion: +10% completed, +30% planned over next year; new COO Brett Carucci

stories.summary: LG Group, a Chicago-based development and contracting firm, announced a restructuring to support $500M+ in new development and $100M in general contracting next year. The company has already expanded its workforce 10% and plans 30% growth over the next year under new COO Brett Carucci. Primary expansion markets are Nashville and Phoenix, with additional focus on major markets nationwide.
stories.impact: A mid-market development firm committing $500M+ to integrated development (likely mixed-use, multifamily, or commercial) in Nashville and Phoenix signals confidence in those growth metros' near-term demand and financing environment. LG's headcount expansion (30% YoY) reflects labor availability and cost optimization relative to project pipeline. For TCR competing in Nashville/Phoenix: track LG's project announcements closely—rapid expansion by regional developers often precedes broader capital competition and cost inflation in those markets. Early-stage land control in both metros is increasingly valuable as development velocity accelerates.

stories.title: ICP Acquires 427K-SF Corporate Campus in Kalamazoo
stories.excerpt: Industrial Commercial Properties LLC (ICP) has acquired 1 Financial Parkway, a three-building, 426,788-square-foot corporate campus situated on 55 acres in Kalamazoo, Michigan.“We continue to see opportunities where good real estate can be repositioned to serve new companies and new uses. We have invested successfully in Michigan for years, and surpassing five million square feet reinforces our commitment tocontinuing that growth and repositioning properties like this one.”The property’s I-1 zoning allows a variety of office and industrial uses, giving ICP flexibility to reposition the existing campus for a broad range of users. Its location along I-94 offers convenient access to Kalamazoo, Portage, and Battle Creek, placing the property on the major transportation corridor connecting Chicago and Detroit.ICP plans to evaluate opportunities to market the campus, with the combination of existing infrastructure, highway access, and developable acreage providing multiple options for future users. The post ICP Acquires 427K-SF Corporate Campus in Kalamazoo appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: ICP acquired 1 Financial Parkway, Kalamazoo, MI: 427K SF, 3-building campus on 55 acres
I-1 zoning allows office and industrial flexibility; located on I-94 corridor (Chicago–Detroit)

stories.summary: Industrial Commercial Properties LLC (ICP) acquired 1 Financial Parkway, a 427K-SF, three-building corporate campus on 55 acres in Kalamazoo, Michigan. The property's I-1 zoning allows diverse office and industrial uses, and its I-94 location provides access to Chicago and Detroit. ICP, which has invested over 5M SF in Michigan, plans to evaluate repositioning and future use options for the campus.
stories.impact: ICP's acquisition of a large, flexible-use campus in Kalamazoo (Midwest secondary market) suggests continued confidence in I-94 corridor logistics and light industrial demand. The 55-acre development-ready parcel with I-1 zoning is a signal that secondary Midwest markets (Kalamazoo, Battle Creek corridor) are attracting institutional capital for adaptive/mixed-use repositioning. Multifamily developers should monitor Kalamazoo job growth and corporate relocations; large flexible campuses often signal employer interest and potential precedes residential demand. Land availability and lower costs in Kalamazoo may create entry-point opportunities for workforce housing development ahead of broader Midwest-bound population migration.

stories.title: Ares Buys Two Fully Leased Miami Warehouses for $109M
stories.excerpt: Ares Management has acquired two fully leased warehouses in Miami-Dade County from BGRE for a combined $108.7 million, property records show. In the larger transaction, the L.A.-based asset manager paid $65.3 million for a 230,147-square-foot, 15-acre distribution center at 3811 West 108th Street, located between Florida Turnpike and Interstate 75 in Hialeah. National retailer Target is the distribution center’s sole tenant after signing a 10-year lease in 2022 with two five-year extension options, according to county records. In the second sale, Ares Management paid $43.4 million for a 142,472-square-foot, 8-acre warehouse about 13 miles south at 13190 Northwest 17th Street, west of the Florida Turnpike, near Sweetwater. E-commerce parcel delivery company LaserShip has leased the entire property. BGRE, formerly called Brookfield Properties, developed both buildings, completing them between 2022 and 2023. Since opening an office in Miami Beach in 2024, Ares Management has been making inroads in South Florida’s industrial market. Last year, it purchased a 230,976-square-foot warehouse in Weston for $56 million as well as a 456,219-square-foot industrial portfolio in Broward County for $121 million. A spokesperson for Ares declined to comment, while a representative for BGRE did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Ares Management acquired two fully leased Miami warehouses from BGRE (Brookfield), $108.7M total
230K SF Hialeah warehouse (Target, 10-yr + options, $65.3M); 142K SF Sweetwater warehouse (LaserShip, $43.4M)
Both buildings completed 2022–2023; Ares opened Miami office in 2024, signals expansion intent
stories.summary: Ares Management purchased two fully leased logistics warehouses in Miami-Dade County from Brookfield (BGRE) for $108.7M combined. The larger 230K-SF distribution center in Hialeah is leased to Target under a 10-year lease with extension options; the 142K-SF Sweetwater facility is leased to LaserShip. Both were recently completed (2022–2023), and Ares' Miami office launch in 2024 indicates strategic expansion in the region.
stories.impact: Ares' $109M acquisition of fully leased, recently built logistics warehouses in Miami-Dade signals institutional capital confidence in South Florida e-commerce/logistics fundamentals and last-mile delivery networks. Target and LaserShip long-term leases provide yield; Ares' Miami office establishment suggests plans for active deal sourcing and portfolio growth in the market. For multifamily developers: robust logistics demand in Miami-Dade (especially Hialeah–Sweetwater I-75 corridor) indicates sustained job growth and wage supports for service/logistics workers; this is a secondary demand driver for workforce multifamily. Monitor industrial absorption and rent growth; tight logistics supply may pull residential growth toward industrial employment hubs.

stories.title: Gaia Lands Another Extension for Williamsburg Apartments’ $48M Loan
stories.excerpt: It’s déjà vu for GAIA Real Estate. The developer landed for the second straight year a one-year extension for its $48 million loan on loan with Raymond James Bank backing a multifamily property at 55 Hope Street in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, Commercial Observer can first report. The extension pushed the loan maturity to August 2027, which will be five years after Gaia acquired the 1907-built and 2012-renovated apartment building previously utilized as a pencil factory. “We acquired the property at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, amid significant uncertainty in New York, and have since increased net operating income significantly through active management and a long-term approach to value creation, Danny Fishman, CEO and co-founder at Gaia Real Estate, said in a statement. “This extension demonstrates our ability to identify opportunities across market cycles and position our investments for sustained performance in Brooklyn’s multifamily market.” Fishman added that lenders were interested in refinancing the loan given that the loan is less than 50 percent loan-to-value with a “very strong” debt service coverage ratio, but he opted to go the extension route due to the current rising interest rate climate. After purchasing the 117-unit property from Hope Street Capital for $80 million in August 2022, Gaia added coworking space and refurbished the building’s rooftop while also providing tenant concessions. Hope Street Capital acquired the building for $17 million in 2010 and converted it from industrial to residential use, The Real Deal previously reported. Raymond James Bank did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: GAIA Real Estate secured second consecutive 1-year extension on $48M loan, 55 Hope Street Williamsburg
Maturity pushed to August 2027 (5 years post-acquisition); Raymond James Bank backing
Asset: 1907-built, 2012-renovated former pencil factory, multifamily; NOI increased through active management
stories.summary: GAIA Real Estate obtained its second consecutive one-year extension on a $48M loan for its Williamsburg multifamily property at 55 Hope Street from Raymond James Bank, pushing maturity to August 2027. The firm acquired the 1907-built, 2012-renovated former pencil factory during the COVID pandemic and has grown NOI through active management. Lender interest in extension signals confidence in the asset's performance and GAIA's execution.
stories.impact: Minimal market-level impact. However, GAIA's back-to-back extension wins suggest that adaptive-reuse and well-managed Value-Add multifamily assets in Brooklyn's strong submarkets (Williamsburg) are performing enough to attract non-traditional lenders (debt funds, bank participation) seeking yield in tight cap-rate environments. Repeated extensions rather than refinances may indicate rising rates, tightened CMBS availability, or GAIA's preference to hold through near-term rent growth cycles. For TCR: adaptive-reuse and Value-Add Brooklyn multifamily remain attractive to lenders; opportunity exists to acquire, stabilize, and refinance similar assets, but monitor refinance windows carefully as SOFR/term spreads remain elevated.

stories.title: Membership Platform Patreon Renews 45K-SF Sublease at 75 Varick Street
stories.excerpt: Patreon is staying put at its offices in Manhattan’s Hudson Square. The membership and monetization platform, which allows creators to build communities and share exclusive content, has signed a sublease renewal for 44,661 square feet at Hudson Square Properties’ 75 Varick Street, according to a monthly office report from CBRE. The renewal was confirmed by Patreon. It’s unclear when the San Francisco-based company moved into the 18-story office building, also known as One Hudson Square, or who the sublandlord is. 75 Varick is a flagship property within the Hudson Square Properties portfolio, which is owned through a joint venture involving Trinity Church Wall Street and Norges Bank Investment Management. Hines was also a minority investor and operating partner in the JV, but Commercial Observer reported in July that it would no longer hold its stake in the 13-property portfolio, and that Brookfield might replace Hines by securing a 10 percent stake in the portfolio. The length of Patreon’s renewal and the asking rent were unclear, but a report from Newmark found office rents in Hudson Square averaged $91.02 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026. The brokers involved in the deal were also unclear. Spokespeople for Hudson Square Properties and CBRE did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Patreon shares its 75 Varick building with several other tenants, including artificial intelligence productivity software developer Notion and creative production firm RadicalMedia, which both renewed leases there in January. In fact, renewal deals appear to be popular at 75 Varick, as media company Horizon Media signed a deal there in March 2025 to keep its 360,000 square feet for another 17 years. And it’s not just 75 Varick — the entire Hudson Square neighborhood has been reaping the benefits of the city’s AI boom and increased leasing demand. stories.summary: Patreon, a San Francisco-based creator monetization platform, renewed its 44,661-SF sublease at 75 Varick Street in Manhattan's Hudson Square. Hines is exiting its minority stake, and Brookfield may acquire a 10% position in the portfolio.

Patreon's renewal in Hudson Square (office) reflects stability in NYC's creative/tech office demand, but sublease activity (vs. direct lease) may signal softening landlord economics or flight-to-quality dynamics. Trinity Church/Norges Bank's control of Hudson Square and Brookfield's potential stake acquisition suggest institutional investors are consolidating NYC trophy office—but this capital is not flowing into multifamily. Watch for office conversions if Hudson Square office leasing softens; conversion potential exists in mixed-use buildings.

stories.title: Developer Ailanthus Files Plans to Build 400 Apartments at 424 Hoyt Street in Gowanus
stories.excerpt: Residential towers grow in Brooklyn. Affordable and mixed-income housing developer Ailanthus has filed a rezoning application with the New York City Department of City Planning to build a 17-story, 175-foot-tall mixed-use residential development at 424 Hoyt Street in Gowanus, Brooklyn. If approved, the building would have 400 apartment units — of which 100 to 120 would be affordable — as well as a 46,000-square-foot public school and 14,000 square feet of commercial retail space, according to the application filing. The application still has several steps to get through before approval is granted. “As noted in the Mamdani administration’s recently released report, New York City needs to create 700,000 new housing units over the next 10 years. While Gowanus contributed thousands of units in the last few years, Community Board 6, which encompasses Gowanus, was identified as one of three districts in Brooklyn with the least access to affordable homes, setting a target for thousands more units to be created there,” a spokesperson for Ailanthus told Commercial Observer. Two Trees Management acquired 424 Hoyt Street in July 2008 for $7.7 million, according to property records. Ailanthus, led by Ofer Cohen, Vivian Liao and Tucker Reed, has a ground lease at the site from Two Trees. Currently, there is a one-story automotive repair building and a vehicle storage facility on the property, which is allowed 91,800 buildable square feet. Two Trees Management declined Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Gowanus has been in the midst of a glow-up ever since its rezoning plan was initiated, not to mention a 2013 environmental cleanup plan designed to transform one of the city’s grittiest areas. The 82-block redevelopment plan passed in November of 2021. There have been several luxury and affordable housing developments delivered in Gowanus, including the Gowanus Wharf campus, 544 Carroll Street and 499 President Street. bullets: Ailanthus filed rezoning for 424 Hoyt Street, Gowanus: 400-unit mixed-income, 17-story residential

stories.summary: Ailanthus, an affordable and mixed-income housing developer, filed a rezoning application for 424 Hoyt Street in Gowanus, Brooklyn, proposing a 17-story, 175-foot mixed-use tower with 400 apartment units (100–120 affordable), a 46K-SF public school, and 14K SF of retail. Community Board 6 (Gowanus) was identified as one of three Brooklyn districts with the least access to affordable housing, supporting the development's alignment with city housing targets.
stories.impact: Ailanthus' large-scale, affordable-focused rezoning application in Gowanus signals continued density opportunity and public support for residential in the submarket. Gowanus has delivered thousands of units in recent years and remains a key growth node for affordable/mixed-income housing. For TCR: Gowanus' public/political appetite for density and affordable housing remains strong, but rezoning timelines are lengthening and public land contributions (school) reduce developer economics. Compete on speed to entitlement in adjacent Gowanus parcels; alternatively, scout non-rezoning-dependent sites in the submarket to avoid approval delays. Monitor Ailanthus' timeline; if approved, expect construction cost escalation and labor tightening in Brooklyn over next 18–24 months.
